newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan-China shipping reform may spark reflagging.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan-China shipping reform may spark reflagging.

text.p: Taipei's move to allow foreign-flagged ships to sail directly between Taiwan and China may force domestic ships from the two sides to switch to foreign flags, officials and shipping executives said on Tuesday.

In an apparent easing of Taiwan's nearly five-decade ban on direct mainland shipping, Premier Lien Chan approved a scheme ending the requirement that all vessels transit Hong Kong or another third harbour when crossing the Taiwan strait.
"Domestic vessels are not allowed, but Taiwan-owned but foreign-registered ships were approved," an official of the sponsoring communications ministry told Reuters by telephone.

Lien signed the proposal in a bid "to win more foreign shipping firms to join our Asia-Pacific operations centre plan", the official said, referring to Taipei's high-profile drive to become a regional hub for major transnational firms.
The proposal for limited direct sailings still needed formal cabinet approval but, with the premier's nod, had effectively been given the go-ahead, the official said.
It remains a question whether China's rival communist government will allow the direct crossings to begin.
Beijing has balked at earlier Taiwan proposals for limited direct links, instead proposing its own rules for management of what it regards as a domestic shipping matter.

Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war ended in 1949. China is wary of accepting any scheme that would oblige it to recognise the sovereignty of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government, which was defeated in 1949.

If the foreign-flagging scheme were to go forward, officials said it would likely spark a rush by shippers on Taiwan and the mainland to reflag their ships under third-country registration, so as not to be left out of the lucrative new business.
"Sure it's a good thing," said vice president Tsai Ming-hsu of Yang Ming Marine Corp, Taiwan's number two shipper.
"But it had better also allow domestic shipping companies," he said. Without such a move, domestic shipping firms would be forced to switch parts of their fleets to to foreign registration.
Another shipping executive, who asked not to be identified, said mainland ships would face the same dilemma -- to hold out for direct links by all vessels or to reflag.
Another ministry official explained that the proposal was a refinement of an "offshore transshipment centre" plan unveiled in 1995.
Under that plan, "feeder vessels" below a certain tonnage would be allowed to make direct crossings, bringing cargoes to ocean-going ships berthed in mainland or Taiwan harbours.

Shipping firms complained that the feeder plan was not cost-effective, prompting the revision to allow direct crossings by oceangoing ships from five Taiwan ports to Chinese ports as part of onward trips to overseas destinations.
The affected Taiwan ports are Kaoshiung, Keelung, Taichung, Hualien and Suao.
Taiwan has banned all direct contact with China since 1949, refusing to accept the legitimacy of the communist government.

Recently, under pressure from thousands of Taiwan firms that have invested more than US$20 billion in China, Taipei has been exploring ways to ease the ban -- as long as the new links do not undermine the island's security.

Under the offshore transshipment centre plan, cargoes could be shuttled directly across the strait from four Taiwan ports that legally would be considered "offshore", or outside Taiwan customs jurisdiction.
Cargoes originating on the mainland would not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs, while those from inside Taiwan would not be allowed to cross directly to China.
